Maladaptive Strategies.value: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Twenty-one-year-old Malik, a bright young chef from a tight-knit African-American family, first found himself staring out a cramped, stainless-steel kitchen window at the dawn of the morning he was assaulted. He had been working the night shift in a busy downtown restaurant when a regular patron, a gruff man in a leather jacket, entered the kitchen, demanding a drink he had never paid for. The man's voice rose, accusations flared, and before Malik could process what was happening, the assailant shoved him violently into the stainless-steel counter, grabbing his face and forcing him into a corner. The sound of the car that the man had driven away in-a low-riding sedan-blared as he slammed the doors behind him. Malik felt a sudden, terrifying loss of control, the sensation that his life was being ripped apart in the span of a heartbeat. After the attack, Malik began to notice how the very things that had defined the night-violence, the honking car sound, and the crushing sense of helplessness-ignited a cascade of distress. In the days that followed, each time he heard a car's horn in the street or saw a stranger's aggressive stance, his mind flitted instantly to that kitchen nightmare. Those triggers sparked the very same maladaptive strategies that had surfaced that night: he started to imagine, with vivid clarity, that he could exact revenge on the man who had assaulted him; he began to constantly scan his body for any sign of lingering injury, as if the assault were still ongoing; and he withdrew from the memory itself, detaching himself as if it were a foreign story. The triggers also made him feel a constant, unfounded sense of threat-his breath quickened whenever he saw someone moving quickly, and even the quiet hum of the refrigerator in his own home seemed a potential signal of danger. Every trigger opened a door that slammed into memory, forcing the assault to return in the flash of a car's engine or the sight of an aggressive posture. Malik's lingering belief that he had betrayed his own values-he was a man who loved cooking and had never imagined himself as a victim-turned into a heavy, negative appraisal of his own life. He felt that others could have stopped the assault, that he was somehow at fault, and that his future was bleak. These appraisals did not simply sit in his mind; they actively pulled him back into the traumatic memory whenever a familiar sound or sight echoed the night's violence. The very thought that he could have acted differently served as a trigger in itself, sending him spiraling into the same memories and the same triggers that had haunted him from the start. The cycle tightened as memory, threat, and trigger fed each other. Every time a memory of the assault surfaced-whether it was the slap of the assailant's hand or the echo of a car-Malik's threat perception spiked, which in turn amplified the urgency of his maladaptive strategies: the revenge fantasies grew darker, his body-checking became relentless, and his detachment from the memory intensified, forcing the images to flare more violently. Each threat heightened the sense that he was never safe, and the presence of even a benign car honk would send him rushing to the kitchen's back door, heart racing. When he could no longer trust that his surroundings were harmless, the kitchen itself became a trigger; the clatter of pans and the hum of the ventilation system now reminded him of the assault, and the memory loop began to dictate his actions more and more. The last piece of the puzzle was the way Malik's own maladaptive strategies looped back into memory and negative appraisals. The vivid revenge fantasies he cultivated were not just imagined retribution; they kept the assault alive, allowing it to surface unbidden whenever a car's horn sounded or a stranger's posture crossed his path. Constant body monitoring forced Malik to feel the weight of imagined harm with each heartbeat, a physical reminder that he had been hurt. The more he rehearsed these fantasies and monitored for danger, the deeper he sank into a sense of hopelessness, as if he were trapped in a future that was perpetually shadowed by the past. In the weeks that followed, Malik's avoidance grew to the point that he stopped inviting friends over, left early from work, and could no longer stand in the middle of his bustling kitchen without feeling on guard. Now, as Malik sits on a chipped wooden bench in the quiet of his kitchen after a long day, he is overwhelmed by the ache of his own fear. He knows that each time he hears a car's engine or sees someone moving hurriedly, the night will replay with brutal clarity. He has become so isolated that he can no longer pretend that his life is still ordinary. It is this relentless cycle-of triggers igniting threats, of threats spiraling into strategies, and of strategies feeding back into the same memories and appraisals-that finally compels him to seek help. He is terrified of never being able to cook again, of living in a perpetual state of alertness, yet he clings to the fragile hope that, with someone's guidance, he can break the loop and reclaim the kitchen-and his life-as a place of peace rather than panic.
